data.howToName: How to boil eggs for ramen

description: Ramen eggs want a jammy yolk: a large fridge egg needs 5 minutes 30 seconds. Times by size, plus the marinade and peeling notes, from the Williams formula.

examples.result: One large fridge egg, jammy for ramen: 5 minutes 30 seconds.
steps: The egg starts at fridge temperature, 4°C, and the water boils at 100°C at sea level.
The jammy target is 68°C at the edge of the yolk.
The formula gives 330 seconds, 5 minutes 30 seconds.

faqs.answer: A large fridge egg takes 5 minutes 30 seconds for a jammy yolk that halves cleanly. A medium egg takes 5 minutes 5 seconds, an extra-large 5 minutes 55 seconds, and a jumbo 6 minutes 20 seconds.
faqs.question: How long do I boil eggs for ramen?

faqs.answer: A few hours gives a light stain; overnight gives the deep brown color and salty-sweet flavor of a ramen shop egg. Peel the eggs first, then soak them in soy, mirin, and a little sugar, turning them once or twice.
faqs.question: How long do ramen eggs marinate?

faqs.answer: Strain it, refrigerate it, and use it once more within a few days. It will be saltier the second time, because the eggs give up some water, so taste it before you soak the next batch.
faqs.question: Can I reuse the marinade?

faqs.answer: It was undercooked by about 30 seconds, or the eggs were larger than you timed for. A jumbo egg needs 50 seconds more than a large one. Add 30 seconds next time and check one egg before you cool the batch.
faqs.question: Why did my yolk run when I halved the egg?

faqs.answer: Peel while the eggs are still just warm, under cold running water, starting at the wide end where the air pocket sits. Slightly older eggs peel more cleanly than very fresh ones, so use the older half of the carton for ramen.
faqs.question: How do I peel ramen eggs without tearing them?

felicityNote: The ramen egg is the best return on six minutes in the whole kitchen. Make a batch on Sunday and the week's noodles are sorted.

parts.meaning: The constant from the egg's thermal properties: density 1.038 g per cubic cm, specific heat 3.7, thermal conductivity 0.0054.
The weight of the egg in grams. A large egg is 57 g (USDA size).
The starting temperature of the egg: 4°C from the fridge, 20°C at room temperature.
The boiling point of the water: 100°C at sea level, lower at altitude.
The target temperature at the edge of the yolk: 68°C for jammy.
The yolk edge factor. The yolk is about a third of the egg, so its edge sits about 69 percent of the way from the center to the shell.

formula.text: Time = 27 × M^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (Tegg - Twater) / (Tyolk - Twater)). For a large fridge egg at sea level, jammy for ramen: 27 × 57^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (4 - 100) / (68 - 100)) = 330 seconds, 5 minutes 30 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Boil the water first
howToSteps.text: Bring a saucepan of water to a full rolling boil. A jammy yolk needs precise timing, so the water must be boiling before the eggs go in.

howToSteps.name: Lower the eggs in
howToSteps.text: Lower each egg in gently on a spoon and start the timer at once. Keep the water at a gentle boil.

howToSteps.name: Time it
howToSteps.text: Boil a large fridge egg for 5 minutes 30 seconds. A medium egg needs 5 minutes 5 seconds, an extra-large 5 minutes 55 seconds, and a jumbo 6 minutes 20 seconds.

howToSteps.name: Ice bath
howToSteps.text: Move the eggs straight to ice water for 5 minutes. This stops the cooking so the yolk stays jammy instead of setting firm.

howToSteps.name: Peel and marinate
howToSteps.text: Peel under cold running water while the eggs are still just warm, then soak in soy, mirin, and a little sugar for a few hours or overnight.

lede: A ramen egg is a jammy egg: a large fridge egg takes 5 minutes 30 seconds, and the yolk comes out thick and glossy, ready for the marinade. The yolk edge reaches 68°C, just inside the range where yolk starts to set.

title: How Long to Boil Eggs for Ramen
tutorial: A ramen egg, ajitama, is a jammy egg with a job to do: the yolk should be thick and glossy enough to slice cleanly in half and rich enough to melt into the broth. A large fridge egg takes 5 minutes 30 seconds to get there. Thirty seconds less and the yolk runs when you cut it; thirty seconds more and it starts to set.

The marinade is the second half of a ramen egg. Peel the eggs while they are still just warm, then soak them in soy, mirin, and a little sugar. A jammy yolk takes up the marinade better than a hard one, because the yolk is still soft enough to absorb it. A few hours gives a light stain; overnight gives the deep brown color and salty-sweet flavor of a ramen shop egg.

Peeling is the fiddly part. A jammy egg is fragile, and the white tears if you rush it. Cool the eggs in ice water for 5 minutes, tap the wide end first where the air pocket sits, and peel under cold running water. Slightly older eggs peel more cleanly than very fresh ones, so save the freshest eggs for frying and use the older half of the carton for ramen.

Size moves the time the usual way: a medium egg needs 5 minutes 5 seconds, an extra-large 5 minutes 55 seconds, and a jumbo 6 minutes 20 seconds. A room-temperature large egg needs 4 minutes 15 seconds. If you buy jumbo eggs for ramen, remember the extra 50 seconds, or the yolk will run when you halve it.

Make more than you need. Ramen eggs keep in the marinade in the fridge for a day or two, and they are just as good sliced over rice or a grain bowl the next day. The marinade can be strained and used once more within a few days.
